technical_errors: Line 151, step 4 classification table: the simulator-divergence row ('Fails on their simulator, passes on the one the profile names as ours') gives 'our-tool, or the other vendor's — do not guess which' as the Usual domain, but 'the other vendor's [tool]' is not a legal value of the `domain` field's fixed six-token enum declared at line 226 and re-affirmed in Human verification at line 292 ('the domain names one of the five, or domain: unknown'). hallucination_risks: None found at high confidence. Every team-specific fact (log paths, marker strings, knob names, manifest location, protocol citation convention) is a [[FILL:]] slot or is read from _shared/team-profile.md by reference rather than re-invented. The Gotchas section rests on general, verifiable UVM/DV domain knowledge (passive vs active agents, config_db set-after-build-phase ordering, null virtual-interface-at-first-use) rather than invented proprietary conventions.
budget_violations: Step 6 (lines 173-179) — the step the skill itself calls the source of 'the most expensive error available in this whole procedure' (misquoting a clause) — budgets only 'One **Grep**' of the Protocol reference document (line 175) with no paired windowed Read, unlike every other artifact this skill touches (log, config dump, integration file, known-issue list, reproduction log are all explicitly Grep-then-bounded-Read). The retrieval budget's own tally, '2 Globs, 12 Greps and 4 Reads' (line 92), excludes any Read for the protocol reference, confirming this is a designed omission rather than a wording slip. review.open_twice: Yes, on balance. The structure, the domain-classification decision table, and the Gotchas section are genuinely useful and technically sound, and the retrieval budget is unusually rigorous and internally consistent (2 Globs + 12 Greps + 4 Reads = 18, verified by line-by-line count). But the bench/not-attempted self-contradiction and the un-Read protocol-clause step are exactly the kind of thing a senior applications engineer hits on the first real escalation (a simulator-vendor bug, or the first time they need to cite a spec clause), and each would cost the file credibility on a second read until fixed.

recheck.why: Lint is clean and scores 1.000 (`skills\dv-customer-escalation-isolation\SKILL.md  [approve 1.000]  clean`), role/level are exactly applications-engineer/intermediate, all 8 declared slots are spent, all 5 claimed profile facts are spent, and the deliberate non-use of Log location and Pass marker is reasoned correctly. The DV content I can check is sound (UVM build-phase config timing, passive agent, null virtual interface surfacing at first use not at connect, finalise-vs-run phasing of an end-of-test check). The handoff block respects the registry: `class` and `phase` carry the full T1 canonical sets, `signature`/`run id`/`owner`/`notes` respect T3 shapes with `notes` last, and `bench`/`bench log`/`domain` are unique in the pack; the claim that dv-escape-analysis uses `repro` with those same four tokens verifies exactly (dv-escape-analysis/SKILL.md:242). But I found four substantive defects, and any one of them is the kind of thing that shows up as an argument with a colleague or a case in the wrong queue. (1) A verifiably false statement about a file in this same repo, in the one paragraph whose whole job is to be a checkable claim about field names. (2) A closed retrieval ledger that does not fund a check step 4 makes mandatory. (3) One word, "ours", carrying two different facts in the routing rule for the `our-tool` domain — the exact hazard this skill polices carefully everywhere else. (4) A missing route to the sibling that this skill's own downstream declares as its consumer. Answers to the numbered questions: 1 — mostly yes, except the "ours" conflation in the step 4 simulator row; 2 — no, step 4 requires evidence no budgeted call can retrieve; 3 — yes, the `spec` cross-reference and the ship/not-ship premise; 4 — yes, every slot is spent; 5 — the block agrees with handoff-vocabulary.md, but `escalation` has no assigning step and step 7's third branch assigns no `known` token; 6 — yes, exact; 7 — yes, 1.000 and clean; 8 — no.
remaining: FALSE CROSS-REFERENCE (line 285-287). The skill writes: "The citation line is `clause`, the same name and content `dv-spec-feature-extract` and `dv-spec-interpretation-ledger` use, so a clause argued with a customer matches one already logged internally; that skill's `spec` field is a *judgement* about the specification, not a citation, so the two must not be merged." Neither named skill has a `spec` field. `grep -rn '^spec *:' skills/*/SKILL.md` returns exactly one hit in the whole pack: dv-escape-analysis/SKILL.md:242 `spec      : clear | ambiguous | wrong`. dv-spec-interpretation-ledger keeps the revision in `document` and its judgements in `authority` and `shape`; dv-spec-feature-extract has `clause`, `obligation`, `observable` and no `spec`. By proximity "that skill" reads as dv-spec-interpretation-ledger and is simply wrong; if dv-escape-analysis was meant, it is named four sentences earlier in an unrelated argument about `repro` and no reader will recover the referent. Either name dv-escape-analysis explicitly or delete the clause.

BUDGET HOLE — step 4 requires evidence the ledger does not fund. Row 7's Check first column reads "simulator and version on both sides, then the compile switches and the timescale", and the paragraph under the table makes it a precondition: "two runs whose compile switches or timescale differ (`customer-integration`). Only if all three are ruled out on evidence, write `domain: unknown`". The ledger is explicitly closed — "The whole ledger is 2 Globs, 12 Greps and 5 Reads — about 19 calls, four of them conditional, and nothing outside it" — and every call is named: the three Greps of their log are the VIP version banner (step 2), the VIP identity markers and the earliest complaint's line number (step 3); the one 80-line Read sits around that complaint, not at the log header. Nothing in the ledger retrieves a simulator banner, a compile switch, or a `timescale directive, and the step 5 integration-file window is spent on knob names. So this row can only be closed by fabricating the check or by spending an unbudgeted Grep.

THE SAME HOLE ALSO BREAKS THE MARKER RULE. To get "simulator and version on both sides" out of their log the agent must Grep for a simulator banner string — but no slot declares what a simulator banner looks like. The profile's **Simulator** fact is "which simulator we use, and the command that launches a build", which is not a printed-banner string, and the skill correctly refuses to reuse the profile's Fatal markers on a customer log in step 3 for exactly this reason. Either add a slot for the simulator banner and fund its Grep, or state plainly that the simulator identity comes from a person and mark the row provisional.

"OURS" CARRIES TWO DIFFERENT FACTS in the `our-tool` routing rule. Row 7: "our-tool only if the failing simulator is ours", and below the table: "When the simulator that fails is *not* the one the profile names as ours, a defect in it is not `our-tool` — we do not ship that tool". The only anchor for "ours" is the profile's **Simulator** fact, which records the simulator we *use internally* — it says nothing about what we *ship*. For an IP vendor running a third-party simulator, this rule routes a third-party simulator defect into our own tool queue, which is precisely the harm the next sentence warns about: "that queue is ours, and the case will sit in it". The ship/not-ship question has a proper anchor already in this skill — the **Release manifest** slot says "which VIP, model and tool versions shipped in a given release" — so bind it there, or add a slot. Do not let one word mean two facts; that is the failure mode _shared/team-profile.md and this skill's own VIP-identity-vs-Fatal-markers paragraph both call out.

MISSING ROUTE to dv-customer-defect-handoff. That skill names this one as its upstream and depends on the handover: "`dv-customer-escalation-isolation` settles which of five fault domains actually broke. Come here when it lands on our VIP or our tool and **carry its record over rather than redoing it** ... Its `signature` and `known` lines are steps 3 and 4 below already done. Its `versions` line is **not** all of step 2". This skill's "When to use something else" never names it. Its own opening promises the output is "either an internal bug with somewhere to go", then routes an `our-vip` verdict to `dv-minimal-reproducer` — which shrinks a reproducer, a later and different job — so the reader who lands on our-vip is sent past the skill that actually builds the defect record. dv-escalation-ownership (same escalation, ownership rather than isolation) is likewise unrouted.

MINOR — step 7's third branch assigns no value. "**Unfilled**: say the check did not happen, and never tell a customer their issue is new." The block offers only `known : known-issue <key> | not-matched | list-not-readable`. The other two branches name their token explicitly ("until then the case is `list-not-readable`"); this one leaves the reader to infer. Name it.

MINOR — `escalation : <our case identifier, and the customer-facing one if they differ>` has no step that assigns it. Step 1 reads the ticket but never says to record the case key, and step 9 only says to write the record.

MINOR — budget item 5 books the bench log as one of "Three further customer artifacts", but it is our own bench's log, not theirs. That is the exact distinction step 9 spends a paragraph enforcing between `log` and `bench log`; the budget should use the same words.

MINOR — budget item 6 says "four of them conditional", counting the two protocol-reference calls and the two known-issue Greps. Step 8's Grep and Read are also conditional ("*if a path comes back*"), so six are. The arithmetic 2+12+5=19 is otherwise correct and every step's named calls reconcile against it.
